summary: This standards-track document describes the Segment Routing architecture, which uses source routing. A node steers a packet through an ordered list of instructions called segments, which can represent topological or service-based instructions. A segment may have local meaning to a node or global meaning in the domain.

eli5.summary: Instead of every road asking where to send you, you carry a list of stops. The packet follows that list in order.

questions: how does source routing with segments work
how does segment routing keep state
subtitle: Steer a packet by giving it an ordered list of instructions, so only the entry router has to remember the path.

tldr.problem: Forcing a flow onto a specific path normally means keeping per-flow state in every router along that path.
tldr.mechanism: The ingress node attaches an ordered list of segments (instructions) to the packet. Each segment is carried as an MPLS label or an IPv6 address, and the node holding the active segment carries it out.
tldr.outcome: Per-flow state is kept only at the ingress nodes of the SR domain. The architecture is later updated by RFC 9256, and it relies on a trusted domain with filtering at its boundaries.

today: RFC 8402 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9256. The RFC itself limits SR to unicast and to a trusted domain with filtering at its edges.

sections.title: Source Routing With Segments
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) uses the source routing idea. A node steers a packet through an SR Policy, an ordered list of instructions called segments. A segment can be topological, such as forwarding out a specific interface or along a specific path to a destination. It can also be a service instruction, such as processing the packet in a container or Virtual Machine, or a QoS treatment, such as shaping the packets at a given rate.

A segment can be local to one SR node or global within the whole SR domain. A segment is often referred to by its Segment Identifier (SID). SR supports per-flow explicit routing while keeping per-flow state only at the ingress nodes to the SR domain.

The architecture works with any control plane. In a distributed setup, IS-IS, OSPF or BGP allocate and signal the segments. In a centralized setup an SR controller allocates them and computes the policies, and it may program the network with NETCONF, PCEP or BGP. A hybrid setup adds a controller on top of a distributed base. Hosts MAY be part of an SR domain.

The document defines the architecture only. It says it does not define how to implement it, which is left to many referenced documents.
sections.eli5: Imagine a treasure hunt where the first person hands you a list of stops. Only that first person has to know the whole route, and everyone else just sends you to the next stop on your list.

sections.title: Segments, Domains and Operations
sections.content:
An SR domain is the set of nodes that take part in the source-based routing model. All nodes in a domain are expected to be managed by the same administrative entity. The active segment is the one the receiving router uses to process the packet.

Three operations describe what happens to the segment list:

  • PUSH inserts a segment at the top of the list.
  • NEXT means the active segment is completed, so the next segment becomes active.
  • CONTINUE means the active segment is not completed, so it stays active.

Two label blocks matter. The SR Global Block (SRGB) is the set of global segments in the domain. The SR Local Block (SRLB) is a set reserved for local segments. In SR-MPLS, using identical SRGBs on all nodes in the domain is strongly recommended, because the same label then means the same global segment at every node.

The document also defines the IGP-Prefix segment (Prefix-SID), the IGP-Node segment (Node-SID), the IGP-Anycast segment (Anycast-SID) and the IGP-Adjacency segment (Adj-SID). An SR Policy can be configured by the operator or provisioned via NETCONF or PCEP, and it can be used for Traffic Engineering, OAM or Fast Reroute.
sections.eli5: A segment is one step on your list. PUSH means adding a step, NEXT means you finished a step and move on, and CONTINUE means keep heading the same way because you are not there yet.

sections.title: Two Data Planes: SR-MPLS and SRv6
sections.content:
The architecture is instantiated on two data planes. With SR-MPLS, SR is applied to MPLS with no change to the forwarding plane. A segment is an MPLS label, an SR Policy is a stack of labels, the active segment is the top label, and when it is done the label is popped.

With SRv6, SR uses a new type of IPv6 routing header, the SR Header (SRH). A segment is an IPv6 address, and an SR Policy is an ordered list of SRv6 SIDs in the header. The active segment is the packet's Destination Address (DA). The next one is indicated by the SegmentsLeft (SL) pointer. When a segment is completed, SL is decremented and the next segment is copied into the DA.

An operator MUST explicitly instantiate an SRv6 SID, because IPv6 node addresses are not SRv6 SIDs by default. Nodes without SR support still hold a plain IPv6 forwarding entry covering the SID, so they can forward packets towards the node that owns it.
sections.eli5: On one kind of network the list is a stack of numbered tickets and you hand over the top ticket at each stop. On the other kind, the list is written in the packet and a pointer moves along it.

sections.title: IGP Segments
sections.content:
An SR-capable node running a link-state IGP advertises segments for its attached prefixes and adjacencies. The IGP extensions that carry them are defined in other documents.

A Prefix-SID is global within the domain unless advertised otherwise. The context for it is the prefix, topology and algorithm, and several SIDs MAY be allocated to one prefix as long as that tuple is unique. This document defines two algorithms. Shortest Path First is the default and follows the ECMP-aware SPF path, though a midpoint may apply local policy. Strict-SPF instructs every router on the path to ignore any local policy that overrides the SPF decision. A source MUST NOT use an SR Policy with a Strict-SPF segment if the path crosses a node that does not support it.

In SR-MPLS the allocation process MUST NOT allocate the same Prefix-SID to different prefixes. If a node learns a Prefix-SID outside its configured SRGB range, it MUST NOT use it and SHOULD log a misconfiguration. An IGP Node-SID MUST NOT be tied to a prefix owned by more than one router.

An Anycast-SID forces ECMP-aware shortest-path forwarding to the closest node of an anycast set. All routers in an anycast group MUST advertise the same prefix with the same SID value. The RFC warns that using an anycast segment without identical SRGBs on all nodes in the group may lead to misrouting, and in an MPLS VPN deployment some traffic may leak between VPNs.

An Adj-SID makes a node switch the packet out a defined interface or set of interfaces, overriding the SPF decision regardless of IGP cost. A node SHOULD allocate one Adj-SID for each of its adjacencies. Its flags cover eligibility for protection, local or global scope (default SHOULD be local), and persistence across control plane restarts. Parallel adjacency suppression MUST NOT be performed by the IGP. When parallel links share an Adj-SID, a weight tells the ingress how to load-balance. In the RFC's example, Link-1 has weight 1 and Link-2 has weight 2, so twice as many packets use Link-2.
sections.eli5: A Prefix-SID is like a street address everyone in town agrees on. An Adj-SID is like saying 'take this exact door out of the building', whatever the usual route would be.

sections.title: BGP and Binding Segments
sections.content:
BGP can also allocate and distribute segments. A BGP-Prefix segment is the BGP equivalent of the IGP-Prefix segment and is global within the SR domain unless advertised otherwise. A likely use is an IGP-free, hyper-scale spine-leaf topology where connectivity is learned only via BGP.

For BGP Egress Peer Engineering, an egress node MAY advertise BGP peering segments. They let an ingress border router steer a flow within its AS towards a chosen egress border router and through a chosen peer. Three types are defined, all local segments with the SR operation NEXT.

A Binding SID (BSID) is bound to an SR Policy, whose instantiation may involve a list of SIDs. Packets arriving with the BSID as active segment are steered onto that policy. A local BSID SHOULD be allocated from the SRLB, and a global BSID MUST be allocated from the SRGB. The policy is stored only on the nodes that impose it, so changing it updates only those nodes and users of the policy are not affected.

One use of a Binding segment is the Mirroring Context segment. A node B can advertise it to offer protection for egress node A. After a failure, a Point of Local Repair pushes the Mirror SID, and B then processes the underlying segments in the context of A.
sections.eli5: A Binding SID is a nickname for a long list of stops. You say the nickname, and the one router that knows the full list does the rest.

sections.title: Security and the Trusted Domain
sections.content:
By default, SR operates within a trusted domain, and traffic MUST be filtered at the domain boundaries. Any node that imposes a label stack or adds an SRH is assumed to be allowed to do so, which the RFC calls a significant change compared to plain IP shortest-path routing. It adds that this is not fundamentally different from RSVP-TE for explicit routing. By default, explicit routing information MUST NOT be leaked through the boundaries of the administered domain.

For SR-MPLS, SR introduces no new behavior in the MPLS data plane. Boundary routers MUST filter external traffic destined to a label associated with a segment inside the domain, including labels in the SRGB, in the router's own SRLB, and labels outside both blocks. For SRv6, boundary routers MUST filter external traffic destined to an address within the SRGB or the router's SRLB.

SR defines no new security mechanism in existing control-plane protocols. Routers accept SIDs only from trusted sources, validated with those protocols' own mechanisms. If these behaviors are not followed or the trust model is violated, the RFC lists malicious looping, evasion of access controls, and hiding the source of DoS attacks. On congestion, SR adds no new requirements and traffic delivery is assumed to be best effort.
sections.eli5: The list of stops is a private map. Guards at the edge of the neighborhood must keep outsiders from using it, because anyone who can write a map can send traffic wherever they like.

sections.title: Manageability
sections.content:
Because the path is encoded in the header and not signaled, OAM mechanisms are needed so operators can check that a path works and monitor its liveness and performance. The document also notes that SR substantially reduces the state in transit nodes. SR OAM use cases and procedures for the MPLS data plane are defined in RFC 8403 and RFC 8287.

Each global segment MUST be bound to a unique index or address within an SR domain. Managing that allocation is described as critical to avoid misrouting, and an implementation SHOULD give a deterministic resolution approach when it detects a conflict. With label stacks, a node may want to signal in the control plane how large a stack it can support. The document says a YANG data model for SR configuration and operations has been defined elsewhere.

In SRv6, managing segment identifiers is no different from managing IPv6 addresses. The Destination Address gives the active segment and the SRH gives the whole path, so the source-routed path can be derived by inspecting the header at any node.
sections.eli5: Since the route is written on the packet, operators need tools to check that packets really follow it. Handing out the stop names carefully matters, so two stops never share a name.
